quizTarget: If both add(2) calls become add(1), what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: An invariant is a rule every usable object must maintain. This Counter permits values from 0 through 3. Private data prevents outside code from bypassing its checked operations.

std::boolalpha prints Boolean results as true or false. The two calls request 2, then 2 more; the second is rejected, so get() returns 2.

reasoning: Both requests fit the invariant: 0→1→2. A rejection would leave the old value unchanged.

quizTarget: Change Session s{12} to Session s{7}. What does duration return?

quizTarget: Insert return 0 inside the nested scope after work. What prints?

Use standard containers and smart pointers instead of hand-writing ownership code. Automatic objects are destroyed in reverse construction order on normal scope exit. Cleanup destructors should not allow failures to escape.

Moving is not reference aliasing. Reusing a after resetting it does not change b. Small scalar moves can just copy; std::move is not a universal speed switch.

quizTarget: Make b a Notebook& alias. How do the reported sizes change?

essentialSupport.fact: The rule of zero: when standard owning members already manage resources, avoid defining custom destructors, copy operations or move operations just to repeat that work.

Notebook contains a std::string and std::vector. Their generated memberwise copy gives an independent name and vector. A struct makes members public by default; braces supply members in declaration order.

Rule of zero is a design preference, not a ban on destructors. A class directly managing a special handle needs deliberate ownership design. Merely adding a destructor can also affect automatic move generation.

reasoning: An alias does not copy the member vector. push_back then changes the single original Notebook.

quizTarget: Replace std::move(p) with p when initializing q. What happens?

In a condition a nonempty smart pointer is true. The comparison p == nullptr checks whether p is empty; this check does not access a missing object.

quizTarget: Omit second.reset(). What does expired() report?

essentialSupport.fact: Copies of std::shared_ptr participate in shared ownership. The object remains alive while at least one owning shared_ptr remains. std::make_shared constructs the object and shared ownership state.

std::weak_ptr does not own the object. lock() returns a temporary shared_ptr if the object is still alive, or an empty one otherwise. reset() releases one owner, not all owners. In if (auto live = observer.lock()), the condition declares live, tests whether it is nonempty, and limits its lifetime to that if statement. expired() reports whether no owning shared_ptr remains.
If objects own one another through shared_ptr, the cycle can prevent destruction. A weak back-reference can break the cycle. Prefer unique ownership when sharing is unnecessary.

reasoning: The weak observer does not own the int, but second does. The temporary live owner is scoped to the if statement.

quizTarget: Call owner.reset() twice. How many times does derived print?

essentialSupport.fact: A unique_ptr<Base> may own a Derived object. For ordinary deletion through Base*, Base needs a virtual destructor so derived cleanup happens too. Removing it here would be undefined behavior; we do not run that variant.
reset() destroys the currently owned object and empties the pointer. Derived destruction runs before Base destruction. Logging is only a visible demonstration of cleanup order.
Resetting an already-empty unique_ptr does nothing. This can be tested without invoking undefined behavior.

reasoning: The first reset destroys the derived object through the virtual destructor. The empty second reset owns nothing to destroy.

quizTarget: Change twice(3) to twice(2.5). What occurs?

Calling twice with 2.5 fails constraint checking instead of quietly truncating it. There is no successful runtime result for that changed program.

quizTarget: Change the capture to [&offset]. What prints in this same scope?

The parameter value arrives on each call; the capture supplies surrounding context. Changing offset after value capture does not change the stored copy.

quizTarget: Replace the second lambda assignment with operation = nullptr. What prints?

quizTarget: Replace a > b with a < b. What sequence prints?

quizTarget: Start accumulation at 10 rather than 0. What prints?

quizTarget: Use a vector containing only 2, then erase it. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A vector operation can invalidate iterators, references and pointers into its elements. Reallocation during growth invalidates all of them. erase invalidates positions at and after the erased element.

Using an invalidated iterator is not a reliable way to see an old value; it can be undefined behavior. This example only reads the newly returned valid position.
